1745.prule: Two primary grammars state the same word-stress rule: stress on the first syllable of the word EXCLUSIVE of (noun-class) prefixes, i.e. root/stem-initial; verbal extension suffixes never shift it; where a C-prefix has fused with a vowel-initial root the fused first syllable carries the stress because the vowel belongs to the root (Schlenker 1864 sec. 11.1-4; Thomas 1916 sec. 7). Thomas 1916 treats tone separately in the next section (sec. 8 'Tones': bi 'hole' vs bi 'black'; sentence tone), so the stress statement is not simply a pre-tonal misreading of tone. Modern sources (Nemer & Mountford 1984; Peace Corps 1987; Kanu & Tucker 2010, following Wilson 1968) analyse Temne as a two-level (H/L) tone language with lexical and grammatical tone and do not discuss stress (neither assert nor deny). Position fixed by morphological structure (stem-initial, prefixes unstressed, suffixes inert) -> set by morphology with a listed exception set; the language is additionally tonal.
1745.srule: None described in simplex words: one accent per word, kept on the stem-initial syllable 'however long, or however polysyllabic the word may get' by suffixes (Schlenker 1864 sec. 11.2); only compound words 'have two accents, when the 2d. is generally the stronger one' (sec. 11.10). Not mentioned in Thomas 1916 sec. 7 'Stress' (p. ix).

1745.tone: Temne is also a tone language. Thomas 1916 sec. 8: 'The role of tones in Timne is comparatively small... Among words distinguished by tones may be cited: bi, hole; bi, black... Tones also play a certain role in sentences'; also 'The falsetto tone is used with monosyllables'. Peace Corps 1987: 'Although Temne is a Tone Language with relative pitch levels (though not absolute) associated with every word, for the sake of convenience. Tone Marks have not been indicated.' Kanu & Tucker 2010: 'Temne is a tonal language'; two level tones H and L, no contour tones (supporting Wilson 1968/2007 against Kamarah 1994, Dalby 1966); tone lexically contrastive and marks definiteness and past tense; downdrift and downstep. None of the three modern sources uses the words stress or accent for Temne (Nemer & Mountford only for English); they neither assert nor deny word stress.

1748.prule: Primary stress is phonemic (lexically specified): it carries high tone, never falls on the initial syllable of a polysyllabic word, occurs at most once per word, most commonly word-finally, and some words (including some monosyllables and disyllables) have no primary stress at all; a non-phonemic secondary stress (mid tone) falls word-initially. No syllable-count or weight rule is given; placement is shown by contrasting word patterns (e.g. /ùlís/ 'rope' final stress vs /ìhùn/ 'nose' no primary stress; /úk/ 'to whimper' stressed vs /ɓò/ 'bench' unstressed).
1748.srule: One non-phonemic secondary stress, realised as mid tone, falls on the word-initial syllable of polysyllabic words, independent of where (or whether) the lexical primary stress falls; the authors treat it as an allophone of non-stress (e.g. ['tā"mákʰ] 'to be sad', ['āsì"mú] 'cucumber', ['kō"kònōn] 'liver', ['īxùn] 'nose').

A 'metrically weak' medial syllable in CvCvCv (3.1.2) conditions raising/syncope but no stress/prominence is attributed to any syllable.

1753.prule: No synchronic accent rule establishable for Tocharian A (extinct; orthography gives no accent diagnostic, unlike TB). Only inference stated: full vowels in a word-initial syllable bore the accent (from vowel balance: a full initial-syllable vowel is never weakened, while second-syllable *-ā-/-a- is weakened/deleted depending on the vowels of the flanking syllables). 1755.dq: It is in the positioning of the stress in individual words (word: basic lexeme and affixes) that the differences between the sociolects and between the absence and the presence of the influence of English (and between varying degrees of the extent of such influence) are most pronounced. (Wurm 1985: 310; word stress sec. 4.2.2 is treated separately from intonation secs 4.2.3ff.)

1755.prule: Word stress on the first syllable (Rural Tok Pisin; 'very strong tendency' per Wurm 1985, 'almost unbroken rule' per Laycock 1985, 'most words' per Laycock 1970); epenthetic cluster-breaking vowels do not count (stress goes to the first non-epenthetic vowel); secondary stress on final -an/-ap/-aut/-daun/-(e)we in words of 3+ syllables; suffix -im does not shift stress.
1755.srule: Not rhythmic; tied to specific endings. Most words of more than two syllables ending in -an, -ap, -aut, -daun or -(e)we carry a secondary stress on that ending, main stress remaining initial (bágaràp [anglicised bàgaráp], tékewè [tèkewé]; also búlmakàu, p. 312, cf. p. 317; the disyllables in the same list are printed with a single initial stress, síngaut, sékan, sánap, púndaun, the ending taking the main stress only in the anglicised variants singáut, sekán, sanáp, pundáun); the stresses stay in place when -im is added (sanapim, singautim, bagarapim). In anglicised/Urban speech the pattern inverts: main stress on the ending, secondary stress on the first syllable in words of 3+ syllables. No other secondary-stress rule is stated, but secondary stresses are also printed on the Rural forms of further three- and four-syllable words listed under (3)-(4) whose less common or Urban variant has the main stress on that syllable (ánanìt, námbatù, ólabòi, píkinìni, pápamàma, tárangàu, málumàlu, márimàri; námbawàn and ólamàn there follow pattern (2)), and p. 317 speaks of 'words which have a main and a secondary stress on non-adjacent syllables such as bagarap..., bul-makau'; no general rhythmic secondary stress is described ('even stressing'). (Earlier, without the syllable-count restriction, Wurm 1971: 7: 'Words ending in -an, -ap, -ap [sic], -daun and -(e)we have a second, often weaker, stress on this ending, e.g. síngáutim = to call somebody, bágaráp = damaged, out of order.')

tn.translation: The Gaulish accent is known to us only in the Romance period, from place names that persisted in French keeping their old accent, and this accent does not conform to the laws of Latin accentuation. ... Judging from the effect it had on unstressed vowels, this accent was an intensity (stress) accent. ... The remarkable preservation of the Gaulish vowels in the words that have come down to us proves that, before the intensity accent, there was a pitch accent, about which we have no information.

1764.dq: The Mojeño Trinitario phonological/prosodic word is defined as the domain of stress, rhythmic syncope and phonotactics. (Rose 2022 AM p.29); 'Preliminary results indicate that the most robust acoustic correlate of word-level stress is intensity, while duration and F0 are less reliable diagnostics for stress (Gordon & Rose 2019).' (AM p.30)
1764.dloc: Rose 2019 §3.1 p.6, §3.3 p.9, §3.4-§4 p.10, §4.2 pp.11-13, §5.3 p.13; Rose 2022 AM 'Prosody' p.29 and 'Stress and rhythmic syncope' p.30
1764.heavy: Rhyme heavy = long vowel or short vowel + coda (Rose 2022); but stress is assigned to URs with open light syllables only; 'a consequence of syncope is that all heavy syllables (CVC or CVː) are stressed, because they result from the reduction of a whole foot' (Rose 2019 p.9) — weight is derived, not a conditioning factor.
1764.prule: Default (>90% of roots): binary iambs built left-to-right over the UNDERLYING (pre-syncope, all-open-syllable) word, final foot may not align with the right edge (final syllable extrametrical); primary stress on the head of the rightmost foot, secondary on other foot heads. = underlying penult in odd-syllabled words, underlying antepenult in even-syllabled words; after rhythmic syncope this surfaces as regular penultimate stress (antepenultimate on the surface when a syncopatable penult is immune). quantity-insensitive: URs contain only light syllables; surface heavy syllables are always stressed only because they arise from foot reduction.
1764.srule: Rhythmic secondary stresses fall on the heads of the non-final iambic feet, i.e. on every even-numbered underlying syllable preceding the primary (e.g. [ˌntan.ˌkow.ˈɾe.po], na.ˌko.pa.ˌja.ka.ˈɾip.ka); they are preserved through syncope and resyllabification, so surface stress clashes are common.
1764.quote: After word formation, the underlying representation is assigned a syllable structure with only open syllables. Iterative iambic footing starts from the left edge, and the final foot must not align with the right edge of the word. As a result, the last syllable is left unfooted in words with an odd number of syllables, and the last two syllables are left unfooted in words with an even number of syllables. Primary stress falls on the rightmost foot, and rhythmic secondary stresses on other feet ... This means primary stress is on the penultimate syllable of the underlying representation in word…

1765.prule: No positional stress rule stated. clit.q: 詞綴與依附詞不同之處在於，詞綴能夠附著的成分通常只有詞，而且有相當的語意及類別限制，並且詞綴常常也會影響其所附加上的詞之重音位置，例如：鄒語詞彙之重音落在倒數第二元音上，故名詞peisu「錢」之重音落在倒數第二元音i上，即peísu；而當詞綴-’u「我的」加綴上在名詞peisu「錢」上形成peisu-’u「我的錢」時，重音則由元音i轉移至元音u上，即peisú’u。依附詞則通常不選擇「寄主詞」的語意及類別，且可以依附在句子中的不同位置

1768.prule: Lexical pitch-accent system (Japanese type): each word is atonic (unaccented) or carries an accent (taki, 'fall of pitch') on the initial, a medial, or the final syllable; location is lexically contrastive (hana 'nose' atonic vs hana] 'flower' final-accented; ha]ru, ku]zira initial; sena]ka, kudamo]no medial). Syllable- (not mora-) counting; in accented words of 4+ syllables high pitch extends from the accented syllable to the penult; atonic words end high. No stress rule stated.

1768.tone: Pitch accent, not stress: Kobayashi analyses Tsugaru with Kindaichi's 'taki' (fall of pitch) whose position (or absence) is lexical, realised per syllable rather than per mora ('syllable-counting syllable language'). The ja.wikipedia account (after Hirayama et al. 2003/Uwano) analyses the same facts with an ascending kernel (昇り核: '津軽弁の場合は、高くなった直後の拍をアクセント核と呼ぶ'), i.e. rise-marking rather than Tokyo-type fall-marking; either analysis is a lexical pitch-accent system with an unaccented class. No statement about stress/intensity anywhere in the source.

1769.prule: Stress and pitch are set up as separate suprasegmental phonemes. All monosyllables are stressed; 'multiple stress' with a crescendo from the first to the final syllable occurs on two-syllable words and on the two principal pitch-pattern classes of three-syllable words; words of four or more syllables crescendo to the 2nd or 3rd syllable and then decrescendo; remaining words carry a single stress that is lexically transcribed (examples show initial, medial and final position: 'coca' initial, 'slats' medial, 'leaf'/'river' final). Three contrastive pitch levels (high/mid/low) with lexical word pitch patterns and minimal pairs (díbá 'poison' vs díbà 'they are'), pitch perturbation under possessives, and suffixes (-a PL, -se NMLZ) with intrinsic stress and high pitch. No positional stress rule is stated.
1769.srule: No 'secondary stress' so named. West & Welch report 'multiple stress' (several stressed syllables in one word) on disyllables, on trisyllables of the two principal pitch-pattern classes and on various other trisyllables, realised as an intensity crescendo from the first syllable to the last (bùpūwɨ́ 'blowgun', yábá 'deer'); words of four or more syllables crescendo to the 2nd or 3rd syllable and then decrescendo; other words have one marked stress. No alternating rhythm or primary/secondary ranking is stated and the authors defer the analysis (p. 11). Revised by Ramirez 1997 sec. 3.6.1, p. 63: intensity stress non-distinctive, placement emphasis-dependent, 'uma certa tendência à colocação do acento de intensidade de duas em duas moras, com muita variação individual'.

1769.cfw: West and Welch's 1967 phonemic sketch of the Acaricuara dialect and Ramirez's 1997 reference grammar of the Brazilian Ye'pâ-masa variety both describe Tucano word prosody as lexical pitch (three pitch levels and pitch-pattern classes in 1967, two tonic melodies against an atonic low melody in 1997) with no fixed stress position, differing only in that the 1967 outline, which defers its own suprasegmental analysis, lists a phonemic stress that Ramirez finds non-distinctive and emphasis-driven.

evidence_works.work: West 1980, Gramática popular del tucano (Bogotá: Instituto Lingüístico de Verano / Ministerio de Gobierno, xii+249 pp.)
evidence_works.note: Pedagogical grammar by the 1967 co-author, written 'para dos clases de lectores' with Tucano speakers first; no elicitation procedure or instrumental data. Agrees with 1967/1972 on three tones (high, mid, low) with only the high marked; adds that isolated monosyllables carry high tone and may lose it in a phrase, that low-high is the commonest disyllable pattern and low-mid-high / low-high-low the commonest trisyllable patterns, and that verbs fall into tone classes A (high on the last root syllable, shifting to remote -a) and B. No word-stress statement anywhere; the 'sílaba que se enfatiza... más fuerte y más alto' at p. 18 is the imperative sentence-intonation pattern, not a word-stress rule.
